17.0.0.en: "Better is a dry morsel, and peace therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife" [1]

17.0.1.en: It is clear that he is speaking of a church community "full of sacrifices." If the Church of the Old Testament was occupied with many kinds of sacrifices, among them the peace offering (Lev 3:1-17), which is "a sweet savour unto the LORD" (Lev 13:5, 16), the subject of God's pleasure is the reconciliation of man with his Creator as with his brethren, that is, practical love.

17.0.2.en: Thus it is fitting for every believer, when he offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, that God will not be pleased with it as long as he carries in his heart hatred toward his brother. Often a person, a family or a church is occupied with enormous activities, but without inner peace; it is fitting for the person to withdraw for a while, to sit quietly with God, to draw from the divine love and to have his heart overflow with love for the salvation of all humanity.

17.0.3.en: God drew Moses out of the midst of Pharaoh's palace, with all its activities, banquets and possibilities, to live in a barren wilderness for 40 years, enjoying a dry morsel and peace with God, rather than living in Pharaoh's palace amid abundant feasts with strife.

17.0.4.en: And Elijah withdrew to the brook Cherith (1 Kgs 17), and left everyone suffering drought for three years and a half, that all might experience the dry morsel and be reconciled to God as to themselves, rather than enjoy good things with strife.

17.0.5.en: Let us withdraw for a while from being occupied with the many church activities, to sit with God as members of the household of God, so that we may enjoy peace with Him, and this peace may be reflected on our relationship with our brethren, and even on the church activities themselves.

17.0.6.en: The Apostle says: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1). "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord" (Heb 12:14).

17.0.7.en: * True peace is from above. As long as we are bound to the body, we bear a yoke of many things that weary us. Seek peace, then, and be freed from the troubles of this world. Acquire a quiet mind and a calm, untroubled soul, not stirred by the passions and not drawn by false teachings, and so defy the acceptance of their enticements, that you may receive "the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts" (Phil 4:7). Whoever seeks peace seeks Christ, for He Himself is our peace, who makes the two one new man (Eph 2:14), making peace through the blood of His cross, whether on earth or in heaven.

17.0.8.en: St. Basil the Great * In the house of God, in the Church of Christ, men dwell with one mind, and continue in harmony and simplicity.

17.0.9.en: * They continue together in prayer, declaring earnestly and in agreement in their prayers that God dwells with those who are of one mind in the house. Only those who are in agreement in their prayers enter the divine house.

17.0.10.en: * God has commanded us to be peacemakers, in unity and of one mind in His house... and He wants us, since we have been born again, to continue thus. Since we have become children of God, we remain in the peace of God, and since we have the one Spirit, we have also the one heart and the one mind.

17.0.11.en: God does not accept the sacrifice of the quarrelsome, but commands him to leave the altar and first be reconciled with his brother, for God is pleased with the prayers of the peacemaker.

17.0.12.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr * For the Lord makes men of one mind to dwell in a house. Hence love alone can endure without disturbance among those who have one purpose and one mind, who together want and refuse the same things.

17.1.s.en: 2. The wise man enjoys the inheritance

17.1.0.en: "A wise servant shall have rule over a son that causeth shame, and shall have part of the inheritance among the brethren" [2]

17.1.1.en: He compares a wise man who knows how to manage matters well with a son who behaves badly. Because of the wisdom and faithfulness of the servant, a man may allow him to be a partner with his sons in the inheritance, as one of the members of his household, while he may give little to the foolish son who is unable to act well.

17.1.2.en: It was in the mind of Abraham to give all that he had as an inheritance to his faithful and wise servant Eliezer (Gen 15:2), had God not given him Isaac. Abraham trusted the servant and entrusted to him all the affairs of his house, whereas Absalom the son rebelled against his father David, and sought nothing less than his neck.

17.2.0.en: "The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts" [3]

17.2.1.en: Afflictions and sufferings for believers are like the fining pot and the furnace for purifying gold and silver. As the psalmist says: "For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried. Thou broughtest us into the net; thou laidst affliction upon our loins. Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads" (Ps 66:10-12). As the Lord says to the house of Jacob: "Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction. For mine own sake, even for mine own sake, will I do it: for how should my name be polluted? and I will not give my glory unto another" (Isa 48:10-11).

17.2.2.en: The goldsmith knows the degree of heat required for the gold in his hands, and the length of time he allows the gold in the fining pot. His eyes remain fixed on the gold in the fining pot, occupied with nothing else, until he pours it out of the pot, pure from impurities. So God will not allow us to be tried beyond what we can bear, but knows perfectly what is for our purity and edification, and His eyes remain in the midst of the affliction, caring for our sanctification and our purification from every impurity.

17.2.3.en: * We know that even the saints, God permits their bodies to fall under the authority of Satan and many calamities to come upon them, and this is on account of slips (for their chastening), because the divine mercy cannot endure that there be in them any filth or defilement until the day of judgment, so He purifies them from every impurity, presenting them to eternity like refined gold or silver, no longer in need of purification. For God says: "And purely purge away thy dross... and take away all thy tin... afterward thou shalt be called, The city of righteousness, the faithful city" (Isa 1:25-26). And also, as silver is tried in the fining pot and gold in the furnace, so the Lord trieth the hearts (Prov 17:3). And also "for whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth" (Heb 12:6).

17.2.4.en: Father Serenus * How glorious are sufferings! By them we are made like His death!

17.2.5.en: As the refiner of gold throws the piece of gold into the furnace to endure the fire for a while until he sees that it is purified, so God permits humanity to be tested by afflictions until it is purified and obtains great benefit... Let us not be troubled or despair when trials come upon us. For just as the refiner of gold knows the time that the gold should be left in the furnace, and takes it out at the appointed time, and does not leave it any longer in the fire lest it be spoiled and burned, how much more does God know this. So when He sees that we have been purified more, He releases us from our trials lest we be cast down and cast out because of the increase of our evils.

17.2.6.en: When something comes upon us that we did not expect, let us not murmur nor let our hearts faint, but let us bear with God, who knows these things exactly, so that He may test our hearts by fire as He pleases; therefore He does this with a purpose, for the benefit of those who are tried. For this reason the wise man commands us to submit to God in all things, for He knows perfectly when to bring us out of the furnace of evil (Wisdom of Joshua 1:1-2).

17.2.7.en: Let us submit to Him continually, and thank Him constantly, bearing everything with contentment, whether He grants us blessings or offers us chastenings. For the latter are a kind of blessing.

17.2.8.en: For the physician is not only a physician when he allows us to bathe (in the baths)... or to go to the delightful gardens, but also when he uses the scalpel and the knife!

17.2.9.en: And the father is a father not only when he caresses his son, but also when he disciplines and punishes him...

17.2.10.en: And since we know that God is more tender than all physicians, it is not for us to inquire into His dealings, nor to demand an account from Him about them, but He does what seems good in His eyes. We do not distinguish whether He releases us from trial or chastens us, for by either way He wishes to restore us to health and make us partners with Him, and He knows our various needs, and what suits each one of us, and how, and in what way we must be saved.

17.2.11.en: Let us follow Him wherever He commands us, and not think much whether He commands us to walk an easy and smooth way or a hard and rough way.

17.2.12.en: St. John Chrysostom * If you are gold, why do you fear the fire, since in the furnace the dross is burned and you come out pure? And if you are wheat, why do you dread the threshing, though you do not appear as what you are except by it, when the "chaff" is removed from you and your origin and honor appear?

17.3.0.en: "A wicked doer giveth heed to false lips; and a liar giveth ear to a naughty tongue" [4]

17.3.1.en: When the heart conceals evil within it, the ears are ready to hear the voice of the enemy of good, that is, the lip of iniquity and its deceptive words; but if the heart is upright, it knows the voice of the enemy of good and refuses even to converse with him. In other words, it is fitting for us not to blame Satan, who casts his nets to catch us, but to blame our hearts, which have turned aside and become ready to respond to the devil's tricks and to take pleasure in his evil thoughts.

17.3.2.en: In the same way, when the false prophets prophesied falsely and the priests ruled wickedly, the wicked people responded to them: "The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so" (Jer 5:31). A person finds pleasure and enjoyment when he meets those like himself, and responds to them. The liar is pleased with the company of liars, and the adulterer responds from the depths of his being to the conversations of adulterers... and so the sinner finds what he can justify himself with and set his conscience at ease by sharing with those who practice the same sin, and on the other hand the wicked support one another in practicing evil.

17.4.0.en: 5 Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished. 6 Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers.

17.4.1.en: "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished" [5]

17.4.2.en: God permits the existence of the poor and needy among humanity so that man may practice his tenderness and love toward his brother; the rich man needs to give, and the poor man gives thanks for the gift of giving which God grants to the rich, so that both groups live in a spirit of love, agreement and harmony together, and mutual respect.

17.4.3.en: It is fitting for the rich man not to despise the poor, for many of the poor are richer than the rich, since by faith they possess within them the Lord Christ, the treasure of knowledge and all learning, and they cherish God's fatherhood to them as a precious treasure, and surpassing eternal glories are prepared for them. Whoever mocks the poor despises these free divine gifts offered to all.

17.4.4.en: * In the Church a person is rich if he is rich in faith, for the believer possesses a whole world of riches. Is it strange that the believer owns the world, since he possesses the inheritance of Christ, which is more precious than the world? "Ye were redeemed with the precious blood" - this is certainly said to all, and not to the rich alone.

17.4.5.en: St. Ambrose * "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker." Why? Because God is the Creator of the poor. He who is cruel, without humanity, so that he laughs instead of being bound to compassion, since he who sins thus is punished for it. This person perishes because he sins against God's high providence and wisdom.

17.4.6.en: St. John Chrysostom If God permits a person or a nation some calamity or affliction, whoever rejoices at the calamity of another falls himself and finds no support from heaven, because he did not have mercy on his brother. The sin of Edom was that it rejoiced over its brethren when they fell into captivity for their chastening (Obad 12-16).

17.4.7.en: St. Ambrose, while he was a bishop, feared lest, having become a Christian and been ordained a bishop, he might perish by condemning some sinner, so he always remembered his weaknesses and set them before his eyes, not to despair but to be tender toward sinners. He says:

17.4.8.en: [I know that I was not worthy to be called a bishop, for I had devoted my life to the world, but by Your grace I have become what I am. And I am in truth the least of all bishops, and the lowest in worthiness. Do not permit him who was lost before his call to the priesthood to be lost when he has become a priest.

17.4.9.en: First grant me to know how to weep with all my inner being over those who sin. This is the greatest virtue, for it is written: "Thou shouldest not have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress" (Obad 13). Grant me always, when I learn of the sin of a fallen man, to suffer with him, and not to rebuke him haughtily, but to grieve and weep, for in weeping for another I weep for myself, saying: "She hath been more righteous than I" (Gen 38:26).]

17.5.0.en: "Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers" [6]

17.5.1.en: There is nothing that gladdens heaven itself like the family that bears the icon of heaven, where every member sees practically in the other members his glory, honor and riches. The old man does not utter a wounding word against the new generation (his children's children), not even in his thought, but sees in them his crown and glory. And the young man does not despise the former generation (his parents), but honors it in a spirit of obedience.

17.5.2.en: Practical love and mutual respect turn the home into heaven, and the family into the household of God, and all touch the promise of the Lord Christ: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Mt 18:20). And where the Lord Christ dwells, all gather together as in heaven from all nations, tongues, tribes and peoples, from all cultures and all ages, and there is no problem of a gulf between generations, but each one sees the reflection of Christ's splendor in the others.

17.5.3.en: * It is said, "Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children is their father." Our glory is the Father of all, and the crown of the whole Church is Christ.

17.6.s.en: 6. Let the believer's speech be befitting

17.6.1.en: much less do lying lips a prince." [7]

17.6.2.en: Some differ in the translation of the Greek word translated here "excellent"; some translate it in the sense of loftiness or sublimity, and others say that it carries the sense of haughtiness and pride. If it is not fitting for the fool to utter lofty and glorious things, then all the more it is not fitting for a noble, a ruler or a leader to bring forth a lying word from his lips.

17.6.3.en: When Saul prophesied among the prophets, "the people said one to another, What is this that is come unto the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" (1 Sam 10:11), this became a proverb spoken when a fool utters lofty things. But the opposite proverb is, in the opinion of some, Abraham, the father of fathers, who denied that Sarah was his wife, for his great station and position made this behavior unbecoming to him (Gen 20:1-13).

17.7.s.en: 7. Giving is the law of the house of love

17.7.0.en: 8 A gift is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it: whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth. 9 He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.

17.7.1.en: "A gift is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it: whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth" [8]

17.7.2.en: If the gift is bound with inner love and humility, it has its own value in the eyes of the one who receives it. The Holy Scripture distinguishes between a gift and a bribe (Prov 17:24); the first is to win a spirit of love and affection, while the second is to pervert the ways of justice, or to obtain things to which we have no right, that is, unlawful things.

17.7.3.en: Jacob's gift to Esau removed the anger and the desire for revenge from Esau (Gen 33:4), and Jonathan's gift to David revealed the attachment of his soul to him, and his love for him as his own soul (1 Sam 18:1-4).

17.8.0.en: "He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends" [9]

17.8.1.en: We begin every congregational, family or individual (personal) prayer by offering a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, the Maker of good things, "for He has covered us." If the Holy One, who cannot endure sin, covers us in order to lift us up with the spirit of hope from our sins, and brings us into His sanctuaries, how fitting it is for His children also to imitate Him, and cover their brethren in order that they may enjoy the holy life. "Charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1 Pet 4:8; compare Prov 10:12).

17.8.2.en: Covering others does not mean flattery or indulgence toward sin, but in a spirit of love, humility and meekness it is necessary to pray for the fallen, that God may cover them and us when we always return to Him. It is also possible to speak quietly with the fallen without wounding their feelings.

17.8.3.en: Perhaps among the most beautiful examples of speaking with sinners is the prophet Jonathan and his dialogue with David the king and prophet for his repentance, where he spoke with him secretly, away from the eyes of others, and with his frankness and firmness he opened before him the doors of hope (2 Sam 12).

17.8.4.en: But whoever "repeateth a matter" (gossip), that is, publicizes the fallen, going about exposing their sins before others, destroys love!

17.8.5.en: * "Ye are the salt of the earth" (Mt 5:13). The properties of salt are many: it makes the insipid delicious, removes the moisture that produces stench, and firms what is soft. So you, draw people and firm up their softness, and warn them lest they incline to hypocrisy.

17.8.6.en: As salt preserves itself and others without corruption and stench, so you be concerned for the souls of the sons of men lest they stink in sin. He called love salt by saying: "Ye are the salt of the earth," that is, you are the love of the earth. So you must be lovers of all people, and be at peace with one another.

17.8.7.en: Ibn al-Salibi * It was said of St. Macarius that he became, as it is written, an earthly god; for as God covers the world, so Abba Macarius covered the faults of his brethren which he saw as though he did not see them, and the things which he heard as though he had heard nothing.

17.8.8.en: * It was said of St. Macarius that a cherub accompanied him from the day he began his ascetic life in the wilderness, strengthening him and giving him power to endure asceticism, and he grew in this every day, advancing in adornment with virtue, so that his good reputation spread throughout the whole Roman Empire and the regions of the East, for in truth he drew everyone to himself for the sake of the practical Gospel life, because of the fragrant aroma of his lofty ascetic labors, until he snatched a multitude of people from perdition so that they obtained eternal life. And our Lord Jesus Christ granted him the gift of seeing the sins of people like oil placed in a glass vessel, and he covered them all, imitating God.

17.8.9.en: The Paradise of the Fathers * Guard your ears from hearing talk of gossip and backbiting, so that your hearts may be pure, for if the ears hear unclean talk, the purity of the heart cannot be kept without defilement.

17.8.10.en: St. Macarius the Great * Nothing is worse for a person than condemnation, for from it he advances to evils and falls into evils; for he who condemns his brother in his heart speaks of him with his tongue and examines his works and conduct, and leaves off looking at what would amend himself, and busies himself with what does not concern him instead of what does concern him, and from here arise contempt, gossip, blame and reproach, and then the divine help forsakes him and he falls into the very thing for which he condemned his brother.

17.8.11.en: Gossip is for a person to tell of the personal sin that his brother has done, saying that he did such and such. But condemnation is for a person to tell of a bad character trait his brother has, saying that he is a thief or a liar or the like, so he judges him as continuing in this trait and not giving it up, and this is a very grave matter.

17.8.12.en: Therefore the Lord likened the sin of condemnation to the beam, and the sin condemned to the mote, and on that account the tax collector was justified despite his iniquities and the Pharisee was condemned for having condemned another, despite his almsgiving, fasting and prayer and his thanking God for that.

17.8.13.en: For judging God's creation befits God and not us, and the condemnation and justification of each one belongs to God alone, for He alone knows the secret of every man and his public affairs, and the judgment that is due in every matter and on every person.

17.8.14.en: St. Dorotheus * By gossip the serpent seduced Eve and brought her out of Paradise, and Adam with her; so exactly like the serpent, whoever falls upon his companion destroys the one who listens to him, and his own soul is not saved.

17.9.s.en: 8. Accepting rebuke and benefiting from it

17.9.0.en: 10 A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool. 11 An evil man seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him.

17.9.1.en: "A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool" [10]

17.9.2.en: The wise man always seeks his spiritual growth and progress in everything; therefore he does not resist a word of rebuke or constructive criticism. But the fool always thinks that he is right, wiser and more understanding than everyone. The first benefits from gentle, purposeful words of rebuke, and the second is not affected even by stripes, for he is rebellious and stubborn, stiff-necked and haughty.

17.9.3.en: An example of this is Pharaoh, upon whom fell not a hundred stripes, but the ten plagues, each more severe than the one before; and yet, even if he was affected for moments, he returned to the hardness of his heart and his stubbornness. He did not benefit from the plagues until the last moments of his life, when he threw himself with his army into the waters so that all died by drowning!

17.9.4.en: We should not wonder if God often permits trials for His saints, as though they were a rebuke He offers them as wise men ready to listen to His divine voice during the trials.

17.9.5.en: It is said that Father Hilarion went to St. Abba Anthony when he was about 15 years old, and for only two months he contemplated his manner of life and his dignified conduct, his diligence in prayer, his humility in dealing with his disciples, his strictness in rebuking, and his counsels.

17.9.6.en: * Must one who rebukes someone tell him the reason for rebuking him?

17.9.7.en: If you do not tell him, how can he amend his condition?

17.9.8.en: If you do not show the wounded man his wound, how will he be healed?

17.9.9.en: Therefore it is better to tell him; but if the souls are weak and cannot hear, we try to tell them in a veiled way and take their weakness into account, just as wine is given to the sick diluted with water, but to the healthy pure wine; so if you find him able to hear, it is better to make him aware of his mistake.

17.9.10.en: If, when you rebuke someone, you yield to anger, you are thereby satisfying your own passion (that of sin), and you must not destroy yourself in order to save others.

17.10.0.en: St. Macarius the Great "An evil man seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him" [11]

17.10.1.en: Here he speaks of the "rebellious evil man," for there are wicked people who fell into evil because of weakness or because of circumstances surrounding them; these need tenderness with gentleness and kindness together with frankness.

17.10.2.en: But the rebellious evil man needs a cruel messenger, because he does not accept the word of gentle, tender rebuke.

17.10.3.en: The Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: "Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; learn to do well.. Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool. If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land: but if ye refuse and rebel, ye shall be devoured with the sword: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it." (Isa 1:16-20)

17.11.0.en: "Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly" [12]

17.11.1.en: To enter into a dialogue or dispute with the rebellious evil man is of no avail, for meeting a ravening beast whose young have been taken from it, such as the bear, is easier than meeting a foolish fool in a state of fury.

17.11.2.en: Always flee from every person who does not cease from arguing in his speech.

17.11.3.en: * If the soul withdraws from all debate, confusion and disturbance, the Spirit of God enters into it, and the one that was barren becomes fruitful.

17.11.4.en: Father Pimen But the wise friend is longsuffering in his discussions, * Abba Anthony was wise, of a brilliant mind, perceiving the reality of people with a penetrating insight, so that those who came to him were filled with amazement to find that he had perceived them as they truly were, despite his seclusion and his distance from people. And his speech was seasoned with heavenly salt, so that his hearers felt a heartfelt joy at the spiritual perfection he had attained, which endeared souls to him and drew hearts to him.

17.11.5.en: Likewise Abba Anthony was distinguished by patience and endurance in discussion, listening to everything said to him and answering it with all balance, so it is no wonder that it was said that God had set him up as a spiritual physician for his countrymen and for all who gathered around him.

17.12.0.en: "Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house" [13]

17.12.1.en: If it is not fitting for the believer to meet evil with evil, what if he meets good with evil? Such a person will not have evil depart from his house, or his family, or his grandchildren.

17.13.0.en: "The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention before it flows out." [14]

17.13.1.en: Negligence over a small spark from a match can kindle fires that spread to burn forests reaching thousands of acres. And negligence over a slight wound can multiply and lead to the death of the whole man. And a small breach in a trench, if neglected, can cause a flow of abundant water that cannot be faced. So if we neglect a sudden anger, and the sun goes down upon our wrath, it is difficult to recognize the bitter consequences in our life on earth and our eternity. Therefore the Lord Christ commands us: "Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him" (Mt 5:25). And the Apostle commands us: "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 4:26).

17.13.2.en: The days of our sojourning are few, short and evil, so let us not waste them in strife. As Abba Aphrahat says: [It is fitting for those who draw near to God to look to Him alone, and take refuge in Him with such piety, so that they pay no heed to insult, even if they are wronged tens of thousands of times.]

17.13.3.en: * He who is wrathful is devoid of longsuffering and love; he is quickly troubled by trifling words, and stirs up strife over a petty, worthless matter, and wherever he has no place he throws himself in... Who does not lament for such a one? He is rejected by God and men.

17.14.s.en: 12. Justice is the law of the house

17.14.0.en: "He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD" [15]

17.14.1.en: It is said: "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!" (Isa 5:20). If God is the Truth, then whoever exchanges truth for falsehood, good for evil, and light for darkness is like one who has denied God Himself, the greatest Good and the eternal Light. So to acquit the unjust and to condemn the innocent is an insult directed against God Himself.

17.15.0.en: 16 Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no understanding? 17 A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.

17.15.1.en: "Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool

17.15.2.en: to get wisdom, seeing he hath no understanding?" [16]

17.15.3.en: Why does the fool hold a price in his hand? Does he want to buy wisdom or acquire it with money? While his heart is not in wisdom, and he does not seek it for its own sake.

17.15.4.en: This is the position of some rich men whose children refuse to learn, and they think they are able to use their wealth and money to get their children into colleges. They may be able to buy academic degrees by one means or another, but their children's hearts do not seek learning or knowledge, and do not care about progress!

17.16.0.en: "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" [17]

17.16.1.en: The true Friend is our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lover of all humanity, who came as a physician for the sick to heal them, and not to condemn them or despise them. And He was born bodily, that is, became incarnate and became man for adversity, that is, to bear the Cross for the sake of the whole world! It is said of Him:

17.16.2.en: "Having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end" (Jn 13:1).

17.16.3.en: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:19).

17.16.4.en: "I came not to judge the world, but to save the world" (Jn 12:47).

17.16.5.en: "And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 Jn 2:2).

17.16.6.en: "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick" (Mk 2:17; Lk 5:13).

17.16.7.en: "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends" (Jn 15:15).

17.16.8.en: "He hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows" (Isa 53:4).

17.16.9.en: * When Jesus is attacked for mingling with sinners and choosing a despised tax collector as His disciple, one of them asks: What benefit can be reached from this? Only the salvation of sinners! The blame of Jesus for mingling with sinners is like blaming a physician for condescending and toiling to find substances with a difficult smell for the healing of the sick.

17.16.10.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Since there is no perfect righteous man, Christ did not come to call those who are not here (in the world), but the present multitudes of sinners with whom the world is filled, remembering the psalmist's saying: "Save, Lord; for the godly man ceaseth" (Ps 12:1).

17.16.11.en: St. Jerome * He showed them that in His present coming into the world He did not come as a judge but as a physician, and did what a physician must practice, by mingling with those who are in need of healing.

17.17.0.en: "A man void of understanding striketh hands, and becometh surety in the presence of his friend" [18]

17.17.1.en: The wise man often warns against rushing to pledge oneself as surety for another without counting the cost and the means of repayment (Prov 6:1-5; 11:15). Paul became surety for Onesimus, and was ready to pay the debt himself (Phlm 18-19). Judah also became surety for Benjamin (Gen 42:17; 44:32). But our Christ, knowing our inability to pay the debt, paid it in advance on the Cross, so that by living faith we might have the right to enter into the divine embrace.

17.17.2.en: His Holy Spirit who dwells in us also intercedes for us, presenting the surety which the Lord paid on the Cross for whoever accepts His love and responds to it. "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them" (Heb 7:25).

17.17.3.en: "The Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. And he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit, because he maketh intercession for the saints according to the will of God" (Rom 8:26-27).

17.17.4.en: "Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us" (Rom 8:34).

17.17.5.en: * When the Holy Spirit sees our spirit wrestling with the flesh, and the spirit withdrawing to the flesh, the Holy Spirit stretches out His hands and helps us in our weakness.

17.17.6.en: Origen Here we wish to make clear that some Fathers see that the intercession of the Holy Spirit here does not mean the essence of the Holy Spirit, but the grace of the Holy Spirit dwelling in us, and the love that has come to us by the Holy Spirit, who directs the prayers of the believers so that they ask for themselves and for their brethren according to the will of God, and what is for their benefit. St. Augustine calls this divine grace "the gift of prayer."

17.18.0.en: 19 He loveth transgression that loveth strife: and he that exalteth his gate seeketh destruction. 20 He that hath a froward heart findeth no good: and he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief.

17.18.1.en: "He loveth transgression that loveth strife: and he that exalteth his gate seeketh destruction" [19]

17.18.2.en: The rebellious man finds pleasure in strife, and satisfaction in foolish, unconstructive argument, and in his rebellion he exalts himself and prides himself on his opinions like one who raises his gates high, so he destroys himself by himself.

17.19.0.en: "He that hath a froward heart findeth no good: and he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief" [20]

17.19.1.en: What a person sows with his twisted heart and his changeable tongue he does not reap good, but evil.

17.19.2.en: The twisted heart cannot offer a holy, upright tongue, but a deceitful, changeable tongue, by which he loses his friends and provokes his enemies, and causes himself countless troubles.

17.20.0.en: "He that begetteth a fool doeth it to his sorrow: and the father of a fool hath no joy" [21]

17.20.1.en: There is no bitterness that befalls a person like having a foolish and senseless son (or daughter), so that joy cannot steal into his heart.

17.20.2.en: * God is called Father, and God's love for humanity is called mother, and it is the cause of the divine Incarnation and His suffering for us. Although God is our Father, He does not rejoice in one who has received adoption without having knowledge of the divine wisdom and knowledge, and who commits evil. But the prudent son pleases his mother, that is, God's love toward humanity. It is she who brings us to God the Father as undernourished (hungry) children longing for strong spiritual food. This is accomplished so that His Son - Jesus Christ - who became like a brother to us (Hab 2:17), may make us citizens of His kingdom, by word and deed, and also our mother the Church, who was betrothed to God the Father by the Holy Spirit. She bears sons and daughters to Him eternally. And those who learn heavenly wisdom and knowledge please God our Father and His Church our mother. But she grieves and laments over the unlearned who do not want to repent and be saved, but prefer to continue in evil.

17.21.s.en: 16. The fountain of joy in the house of love

17.21.0.en: 21 He that begetteth a fool doeth it to his sorrow: and the father of a fool hath no joy. 22 A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.

17.22.0.en: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones" [22].

17.22.1.en: There is nothing that breaks down the body of man like gloom, anxiety and bitterness of soul. But if the heart is filled with the joy of the Spirit, the soul rejoices, and its rejoicing is reflected even on the health of the body.

17.22.2.en: Offering a sacrifice of joy, thanksgiving and praise daily, day and night, turns the believer into something like a rejoicing angel, who defies not only sickness but even bodily death! The believer repeats: "For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living" (Ps 116:8-9).

17.22.3.en: * Every gospel brings joy for a good reason.

17.22.4.en: Origen * He did not fear but rejoiced to see him, because in him is the love that casteth out fear (1 Jn 4:18). He did not say: "He rejoiced because he saw," but he said: "He rejoiced because he sees," believing under all circumstances, and rejoicing in the hope of seeing with understanding. "And he saw it, and was glad"... If those whose bodily eyes were opened by the Lord rejoiced, what joy was his who saw with the eyes of his soul the ineffable Light, the Word who dwells (in the Father), the splendor that dazzles the minds of the godly, the Wisdom that does not fall, God abiding in the Father, and at the same time saw Him coming in the flesh without withdrawing from the bosom of the Father? All this Abraham saw.

17.23.0.en: "A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment" [23]

17.23.1.en: Often the bribe (a gift with a wrong intention) blinds the eyes of those in authority, so they pass unjust judgments. Therefore it is not fitting to offer a bribe to obtain what we have no right to, nor to accept a bribe from anyone, lest we turn aside from truth and justice.

17.24.0.en: 24 Wisdom is before him that hath understanding; but the eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth. 25 A foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him. 26 Also to punish the just is not good, nor to strike princes for equity. 27 He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit. 28 Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding.

17.24.1.en: "Wisdom is before him that hath understanding; but the eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth" [24]

17.24.2.en: What occupies the mind of the wise and godly man is the knowledge of God and the heavenly mysteries, that he may walk by it, with it and to it. But the fool has no aim. His eyes roam right and left without purpose, so he can never come to the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim 3:7; 4:3-4).

17.24.3.en: "Wisdom is God's revelation of Himself to us; we acquire it, and so we carry divine wisdom and heavenly knowledge. St. Augustine sees that wisdom is the ability to taste spiritual realities, and enjoying the truth leads to the glory of God and worshiping Him with the fear of sons. St. John Chrysostom sees that wisdom is the Gospel, that is, the enjoyment of God's joyful plan of salvation. Knowledge, on the other hand, is departing from evil (Job 28:28), and offering the word of salvation to men.

17.24.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the aim of the spiritual man who has knowledge (the Gnostic) is to know God (the Truth) and see Him face to face, that is, to pass over to the perfection of knowledge of divine things through faith, and this through the experience of a pure life and constant contemplation. If we have passed from paganism to faith, it is fitting for us to pass from faith to knowledge, to see God and know Him. This knowledge is a divine gift that we receive through the Son, by receiving Him and being made like Him; that is, through purity of heart we behold God and perceive what seems to others imperceptible.

17.24.5.en: * Gnosis, which is the knowledge and perception of present, future and past things as certain and trustworthy matters, is granted and declared by the Son of God, who is "Wisdom."

17.25.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria A foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him." [25].

17.25.1.en: The wise man often repeats such a statement, affirming that negligence in guiding children reflects bitterness and grief upon the parents, as happened with Eli the priest, who, because of his negligence in bringing up his two sons, saw the two sons killed, the people defeated, and their father die.

17.26.0.en: "Also to punish the just is not good, nor to strike princes for equity" [26]

17.26.1.en: The perversion of justice on the part of a ruler, leader or judge, causing loss to an innocent person or insult to an upright noble, is a detestable thing.

17.27.0.en: "He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit" [27]

17.27.1.en: The wise man, with all the knowledge he has, has few words, and they have their weight, their dignity, and also their clear purpose.

17.27.2.en: * Let your words be measured, reckoned by yourself, knowing that you will give account to God for what comes out of your mouth, including jesting or a word that is not for edification.

17.27.3.en: St. Pachomius * Whoever seeks to know what the will of God is seeks wisdom, and shows himself prudent.

17.27.4.en: Whoever curtails his words to enter into knowledge - if one seeks wisdom, desiring to learn something about wisdom, while another does not seek wisdom, since he does not want to learn anything about wisdom, and even prevents his relatives from doing this, the first is more prudent than the latter.

17.28.0.en: St. Hippolytus of Rome "Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding" [28]

17.28.1.en: Since fools and the foolish are marked by much speaking, without reckoning or purpose, and it is very hard for them to confess their folly, therefore if they keep silent they are counted wise, and if they close their lips they are considered men of understanding.

17.28.2.en: * As in a house when the door is shut, the members hidden in it are not known, so in general we say, if a fool holds to keeping his composure (in silence), it does not appear whether he is wise or foolish. This happens as long as he does not practice a work that reveals what is in the mind of that silent one... And it was said of Solomon: "A fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise."

17.28.4.en: Let the Kingdom of love be established within me!

17.28.5.en: * Let Your temple be established in my depths, the spacious house of love, to embrace all in it.

17.28.6.en: What sacrifice shall I offer You, and what offering shall be smelled as a sweet savour, but the sacrifice of praise and the offering of love?

17.28.7.en: Grant me Your love, that my heart may be filled with Your surpassing peace!

17.28.8.en: I will enjoy peace with You and with Your creation beloved to You.

17.28.9.en: * Break into my heart, O Beloved, for it is Your house, most dear to You.

17.28.10.en: You deposit in it from the treasures of Your knowledge and Your mysteries, so that I may truly become a heavenly storehouse!

17.28.11.en: * That I may live with You, O Crucified One.

17.28.12.en: That I may find sweet the fellowship of Your sufferings, and receive the honor of being crucified with You!

17.28.13.en: For there is no way to fellowship in Your glories except by accepting Your sufferings with joy and rejoicing!

17.28.14.en: * Your dwelling in me establishes Your righteousness within me.

17.28.15.en: Let evil have no place in my heart, nor lying any room on my lips!
